Main.sentence: David Howell Petraeus ( /pɪˈtreɪ.əs/ ; born 7 November 1952) is a retired ___E:United States Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army)___ ___E:general U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_(United_States))___ who served as the fourth ___E:director of the Central Intelligence Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_the_Central_Intelligence_Agency)___ (CIA) from September 2011  until his resignation in November 2012.  Prior to his assuming the directorship of the CIA, Petraeus served 37 years in the ___E:United States Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army)___ .

His last assignments in the Army were as commander of the ___E:International Security Assistance Force U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Security_Assistance_Force)___ (ISAF) and commander, U.S.

Forces – Afghanistan (USFOR-A) from July 2010 to July 2011. His other ___E:four-star U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4_star_rank)___ assignments include serving as the 10th commander, ___E:U.S. Central Command U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Central_Command)___ (USCENTCOM) from October 2008 to June 2010, and as commanding general, ___E:Multi-National Force – Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinational_Force_Iraq)___ (MNF-I) from February 2007 to September 2008.  As commander of MNF-I, Petraeus oversaw all ___E:coalition forces U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-National_Force_%E2%80%93_Iraq)___ in Iraq.

Petraeus was the ___E:General George C. Marshall U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Marshall)___ Award winner as the top graduate of the ___E:U.S. Army Command and General Staff College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army_Command_and_General_Staff_College)___ class of 1983.  He later served as assistant professor of international relations at the ___E:United States Military Academy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Military_Academy)___ and also completed a fellowship at ___E:Georgetown University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown_University)___ .

Since 2022, he has taught courses in ___E:international relations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_relations)___ at ___E:Yale University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yale_University)___ as a Kissinger Senior Fellow of the university's ___E:Jackson Institute for Global Affairs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jackson_Institute_for_Global_Affairs)___ .
Petraeus has repeatedly stated that he has no plans to run for elected political office.

On 23 June 2010, president ___E:Barack Obama U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama)___ nominated Petraeus to succeed General ___E:Stanley McChrystal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanley_McChrystal)___ as commanding general of the ___E:International Security Assistance Force U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Security_Assistance_Force)___ in ___E:Afghanistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_Afghanistan_(2001%E2%80%93present))___ , technically a step down from his position as Commander of ___E:United States Central Command U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Central_Command)___ , which oversees the military efforts in Afghanistan, Pakistan, ___E:Central Asia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Asia)___ , the ___E:Arabian Peninsula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula)___ , and ___E:Egypt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt)___ .
On 30 June 2011, Petraeus was unanimously confirmed as the ___E:director of the CIA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_the_Central_Intelligence_Agency)___ by the U.S.
Senate 94–0.  Petraeus relinquished command of U.S. and ___E:NATO U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO)___ forces in Afghanistan on 18 July 2011, and retired from the U.S.

Army on 31 August 2011.  On 9 November 2012, he resigned from his position as director of the CIA, citing his extramarital affair with his biographer ___E:Paula Broadwell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Broadwell)___ , which was discovered in the course of an ___E:Federal Bureau of Investigation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation)___ (FBI) investigation.

In January 2015, officials reported that the FBI and the ___E:Department of Justice U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/US_Department_of_Justice)___ (DOJ) prosecutors had recommended bringing felony charges against Petraeus for providing ___E:classified information U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classified_information_in_the_United_States)___ to Broadwell while serving as director of the CIA.  Eventually, Petraeus pleaded guilty to one misdemeanor charge of ___E:mishandling classified information U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mishandling_of_US_classified_information)___ .
He was later sentenced to two years of probation and fined US$100,000 for the unauthorized removal and retention of classified material he gave to Broadwell.

Petraeus was born in ___E:Cornwall-on-Hudson, New York U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall-on-Hudson,_New_York)___ , the son of Miriam Sweet (née Howell), a librarian, and Sixtus Petraeus, a sea captain.

His father was a ___E:Dutch U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_people)___ merchant mariner who immigrated to the United States at the start of World War II,  from ___E:Franeker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franeker)___ , the ___E:Netherlands U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands)___ ,   and his mother was American, a resident of Brooklyn, New York.  They met at the ___E:Seamen's Church Institute of New York and New Jersey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seamen%27s_Church_Institute_of_New_York_and_New_Jersey)___ and married.

Sixtus Petraeus commanded a ___E:Liberty ship U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberty_ship)___ for the U.S. for the duration of World War II.  The family moved after the war, settling in Cornwall-on-Hudson, where Petraeus grew up and graduated from ___E:Cornwall Central High School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornwall_Central_High_School)___ in 1970.

Petraeus went on to the ___E:United States Military Academy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Military_Academy)___ at ___E:West Point U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Point,_New_York)___ .

Petraeus was on the intercollegiate soccer and ski teams, was a cadet captain on the brigade staff, and was a "distinguished cadet" academically, graduating in the top 5% of the Class of 1974 (ranked 40th overall).
In the class yearbook, Petraeus was remembered as "always going for it in sports, academics, leadership, and even his social life".

While a cadet, Petraeus started dating the daughter of Army General ___E:William A. Knowlton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_A._Knowlton)___ (the West Point superintendent at the time), ___E:Holly U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holly_Petraeus)___ .
Two months after Petraeus graduated, they married.

Holly, who is multi-lingual, was a ___E:National Merit Scholar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Merit_Scholarship_Program)___ in high school, and graduated summa cum laude from ___E:Dickinson College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickinson_College)___ .
They have a daughter and son, Anne and Stephen.

Petraeus administered the ___E:oath of office U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Uniformed_Services_Oath_of_Office)___ at his son's 2009 commissioning into the Army after his son's graduation from the ___E:Massachusetts Institute of Technology U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Institute_of_Technology)___ .

His son went on to serve as an officer in ___E:Afghanistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan)___ as a member of 3rd Platoon, Alpha Company, 1st Battalion, ___E:503rd Infantry Regiment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/503rd_Infantry_Regiment)___ , ___E:173rd Airborne Brigade Combat Team U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/173rd_Airborne_Brigade_Combat_Team)___ .
Petraeus's residence is a small property in the ___E:Springfield, New Hampshire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springfield,_New_Hampshire)___ , which his wife inherited from her family.
Petraeus once told a friend that he was a ___E:Rockefeller Republican U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Republican)___ .

Petraeus graduated from ___E:West Point U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Point)___ in 1974, receiving a ___E:B.S. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor_of_Science)___ degree in ___E:Military Science U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_Science)___ .

He earned the General ___E:George C. Marshall U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_C._Marshall)___ Award as the top graduate of the ___E:U.S. Army Command and General Staff College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Command_and_General_Staff_College)___ Class of 1983 at ___E:Fort Leavenworth U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Leavenworth)___ , ___E:Kansas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kansas)___ .

He subsequently earned an ___E:M.P.A. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Master_of_Public_Administration)___ degree in 1985 and a ___E:Ph.D. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doctor_of_Philosophy)___ in ___E:international relations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_relations)___ and ___E:economics U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economics)___ in 1987 from ___E:Princeton University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princeton_University)___ 's ___E:Woodrow Wilson School of Public and International Affairs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodrow_Wilson_School_of_Public_and_International_Affairs)___ , where he was mentored by Richard H. Ullman, an international relations scholar and progressive commentator.

At that time, he also served as an assistant professor of international relations at the ___E:U.S. Military Academy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Military_Academy)___ from 1985 to 1987. His doctoral dissertation was titled "The American Military and the Lessons of ___E:Vietnam U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam)___ : A Study of Military Influence and the Use of Force in the Post-Vietnam Era".

He completed a military fellowship at ___E:Georgetown University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgetown_University)___ 's ___E:Edmund A. Walsh School of Foreign Service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmund_A._Walsh_School_of_Foreign_Service)___ in 1994–1995,  although he was called away early to serve in Haiti as the Chief of Operations for NATO there in early 1995. [citation needed]

From late 2005 through February 2007,  Petraeus served as commanding general of Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, and the ___E:U.S. Army Combined Arms Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army_Combined_Arms_Center)___ (CAC) located there.

As commander of CAC, Petraeus was responsible for oversight of the ___E:Command and General Staff College U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Command_and_General_Staff_College)___ and seventeen other schools, centers, and training programs as well as for developing the Army's doctrinal manuals, training the Army's officers, and supervising the Army's center for the collection and dissemination of lessons learned.

During his time at CAC, Petraeus and Marine ___E:Lt. Gen. James F. Amos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_F._Amos)___ jointly oversaw the publication of ___E:Field Manual U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Army_Field_Manuals)___ 3–24, Counterinsurgency , the body of which was written by an unusually diverse group of military officers, academics, human rights advocates, and journalists who had been assembled by Petraeus and Amos.
At both Fort Leavenworth and throughout the military's schools and training programs, Petraeus integrated the study of counterinsurgency into lesson plans and training exercises.

In recognition of the fact that soldiers in Iraq often performed duties far different from those for which they trained, Petraeus stressed the importance of teaching soldiers how to think and how to fight, and the need to foster flexibility and adaptability in leaders.

Petraeus called this change the most significant part of ___E:The Surge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War_troop_surge_of_2007)___ , saying in 2016, "the surge that mattered most was the surge of ideas.

It was the change of strategy, and in many respects, this represented quite a significant change to what it was we were doing before the surge."  Petraeus has been called "the world's leading expert in counter-insurgency warfare".

Later, having refined his ideas on counterinsurgency based on the implementation of the new ___E:counterinsurgency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterinsurgency)___ doctrine in Iraq, he published both in Iraq as well as in the Sep/Oct 2008 edition of Military Review his "Commander's Counterinsurgency Guidance" to help guide leaders and units in the Multi-National Force-Iraq.
Upon his graduation from West Point in 1974, Petraeus was commissioned an infantry officer.

After completing ___E:Ranger School U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ranger_School)___ (Distinguished Honor Graduate and other honors), Petraeus was assigned to the ___E:509th Airborne Battalion Combat Team U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/509th_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States))___ , a light infantry unit stationed in ___E:Vicenza U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicenza)___ , Italy.

Ever since, ___E:light infantry U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_infantry)___ has been at the core of his career, punctuated by assignments to ___E:mechanized units U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armoured_warfare)___ , unit commands, staff assignments, and educational institutions.

After leaving the 509th as a ___E:first lieutenant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._first_lieutenant)___ ,  Petraeus began a brief association with mechanized units when he became assistant operations officer on the staff of the 2nd Brigade, ___E:24th Infantry Division (Mechanized) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24th_Infantry_Division_(United_States))___ , at ___E:Fort Stewart U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Stewart)___ , ___E:Georgia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgia_(U.S._state))___ .

In 1979, he assumed command of a ___E:company U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Company_(military_unit))___ in the same division: A Company, 2nd Battalion, 19th Infantry Regiment (Mechanized), and then served as that battalion's operations officer, a major's position that he held as a junior captain.

In 1981, Petraeus became ___E:aide-de-camp U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aide-de-camp)___ to ___E:General John Galvin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Galvin_(general))___ , then commanding general of the ___E:24th Infantry Division (Mechanized) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/24th_Infantry_Division_(Mechanized))___ .
He spent the next few years furthering his military and civilian education, including spending 1982–83 at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, attending the Command and General Staff College.
At graduation in 1983, he was the General George C. Marshall Award winner as the top graduate of the U.S.
Army Command and General Staff College.
From 1983 to 1985, he was at Princeton; and 1985–87 at West Point.

After earning his Ph.D. and teaching at West Point, Petraeus continued up the command ladder, serving as military assistant to Gen. John Galvin, the ___E:Supreme Allied Commander in Europe U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Headquarters_Allied_Powers_Europe)___ .
From there, he moved to the ___E:3rd Infantry Division (Mechanized) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3rd_Infantry_Division_(United_States))___ .
During 1988–1989, he served as operations officer to the 3rd Infantry Division (Mechanized)'s ___E:30th Infantry Regiment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/30th_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States))___ .
He was then posted as an aide and assistant executive officer to the U.S.
Army Chief of Staff, General ___E:Carl Vuono U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carl_Vuono)___ , in Washington, D.C.

Upon promotion to ___E:lieutenant colonel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant_colonel_(United_States))___ , Petraeus moved from the office of the chief of staff to ___E:Fort Campbell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Campbell)___ , ___E:Kentucky U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kentucky)___ , where he commanded the ___E:101st Airborne Division (Air Assault) U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/101st_Airborne_Division)___ 's 3rd Battalion ___E:187th Infantry Regiment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/187th_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States))___ , known as the "Iron Rakkasans", [citation needed] from 1991 to 1993. In 1991 he was accidentally shot in the chest with an ___E:M-16 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M16_rifle)___ rifle during a ___E:live-fire exercise U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Live-fire_exercise)___ when a soldier tripped and his rifle discharged.

He was taken to ___E:Vanderbilt University Medical Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanderbilt_University_Medical_Center)___ , ___E:Nashville U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nashville,_Tennessee)___ , ___E:Tennessee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tennessee)___ , where he was operated on by future ___E:U.S. Senator U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate)___ ___E:Bill Frist U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Frist)___ .
The hospital released him early after he did fifty ___E:push-ups U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Push-up)___ without resting, just a few days after the accident.

During 1993–94, Petraeus continued his long association with the 101st Airborne Division (Air Assault) as the division's assistant chief of staff, G-3 (plans, operations, and training) and installation director of plans, training, and mobilization (DPTM).

In 1995, he was assigned to the ___E:United Nations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations)___ Mission in ___E:Haiti U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haiti)___ Military Staff as its chief operations officer during ___E:Operation Uphold Democracy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Uphold_Democracy)___ .

His next command, from 1995 to 1997, was the 1st Brigade, ___E:82nd Airborne Division U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/82nd_Airborne_Division)___ , centered on the ___E:504th Parachute Infantry Regiment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/504th_Infantry_Regiment_(United_States))___ .

At that post, his brigade's training cycle at ___E:Fort Polk's Joint Readiness Training Center U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Polk)___ for low-intensity warfare was chronicled by novelist and military enthusiast ___E:Tom Clancy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Clancy)___ in his book Airborne .

From 1997 to 1999, Petraeus served in ___E:the Pentagon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pentagon)___ as executive assistant to the director of the Joint Staff and then to the ___E:Chairman of the Joint Chiefs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Joint_Chiefs_of_Staff)___ , Gen. ___E:Henry Shelton U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Shelton)___ , who described Petraeus as "a high-energy individual who likes to lead from the front, in any field, he is going into".

In 1999, as a ___E:brigadier general U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigadier_general_(United_States))___ , Petraeus returned to the 82nd, serving as the assistant division commander for operations and then, briefly, as acting commanding general.

During his time with the 82nd, he deployed to ___E:Kuwait U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuwait)___ as part of ___E:Operation Desert Spring U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Desert_Spring)___ , the continuous rotation of combat forces through Kuwait during the decade after the ___E:Gulf War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_War)___ .

From the 82nd, he moved on to serve as chief of staff of ___E:XVIII Airborne Corps U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/XVIII_Airborne_Corps)___ at ___E:Fort Bragg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Bragg,_North_Carolina)___ during 2000–2001. In 2000, Petraeus suffered his second major injury, when, during a civilian ___E:skydiving U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skydiving)___ jump, his parachute collapsed at low altitude due to a hook turn, resulting in a hard landing that broke his pelvis.

He was selected for promotion to ___E:major general U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_general_(United_States))___ in 2001.  During 2001–2002, as a brigadier general, Petraeus served a ten-month tour in ___E:Bosnia and Herzegovina U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bosnia_and_Herzegovina)___ as part of ___E:Operation Joint Forge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Joint_Forge)___ .

In Bosnia, he was the ___E:NATO U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO)___ ___E:Stabilization Force U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SFOR)___ assistant chief of staff for operations as well as the deputy commander of the U.S.

Joint Interagency Counter-Terrorism Task Force, a command created after the ___E:9/11 attacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks)___ to add counterterrorism capability to the U.S. forces attached to the NATO command in Bosnia.
In 2004, he was promoted to lieutenant general.
In 2007, he was promoted to General.

On 23 April 2008, Secretary of Defense Gates announced that President Bush was nominating General Petraeus to command ___E:U.S. Central Command U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Central_Command)___ (USCENTCOM), headquartered in ___E:Tampa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tampa)___ , Florida.

In 2010, Petraeus was nominated to command the ___E:International Security Assistance Force U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Security_Assistance_Force)___ in ___E:Afghanistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afghanistan)___ , which required ___E:Senate confirmation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_positions_filled_by_presidential_appointment_with_Senate_confirmation)___ .

He was confirmed on 30 June 2010,  and took over command from temporary commander ___E:Lieutenant-General U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lieutenant-General_(United_Kingdom))___ ___E:Sir Nick Parker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sir_Nick_Parker)___ on 4 July 2010.

In 2003, Petraeus, then a major general, saw combat for the first time when he commanded the 101st Airborne Division during ___E:V Corps's U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/V_Corps_(United_States))___ drive to ___E:Baghdad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baghdad)___ .

In a campaign chronicled in detail by ___E:Pulitzer Prize U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pulitzer_Prize)___ -winning author ___E:Rick Atkinson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Atkinson)___ of The Washington Post in the book In the Company of Soldiers , Petraeus led his division through fierce fighting south of ___E:Baghdad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baghdad)___ , in ___E:Karbala U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karbala)___ , ___E:Hilla U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Hillah)___ and ___E:Najaf U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Najaf)___ .

Following the ___E:fall of Baghdad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_invasion_of_Baghdad)___ , the division conducted the longest ___E:heliborne assault U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_helicopters)___ on record in order to reach ___E:Nineveh Governorate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineveh_Governorate)___ , where it would spend much of 2003. The 1st Brigade was responsible for the area ___E:south of Mosul U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nineveh_Governorate)___ , the 2nd Brigade for the city itself, and the 3rd Brigade for the region stretching toward the ___E:Syrian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Syria)___ border.

An often-repeated story of Petraeus's time with the 101st is his asking of ___E:embedded U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Embedded_journalist)___ The Washington Post ___E:reporter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reporter)___ ___E:Rick Atkinson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rick_Atkinson)___ to "Tell me how this ends",  an anecdote he and other journalists have used to portray Petraeus as an early recognizer of the difficulties that would follow the fall of Baghdad.

In ___E:Mosul U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosul)___ , a city of nearly two million people, Petraeus and the 101st employed classic counterinsurgency methods to build security and stability, including conducting targeted ___E:kinetic operations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinetic_operation)___ and using force judiciously, jump-starting the economy, building local security forces, staging elections for the city council within weeks of their arrival, overseeing a program of ___E:public works U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_works)___ , reinvigorating the political process,    and launching 4,500 ___E:reconstruction projects in Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconstruction_of_Iraq)___ .

This approach can be attributed to Petraeus, who had been steeped in nation-building during his previous tours in nations such as Bosnia and Haiti and thus approached nation-building as a central military mission and who was "prepared to act while the civilian authority in Baghdad was still getting organized", according to Michael Gordon of The New York Times .
Some Iraqis gave Petraeus the nickname ' ___E:King David U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_David)___ ',   which was later adopted by some of his colleagues.
In 2004, Newsweek stated that "It's widely accepted that no force worked harder to win Iraqi hearts and minds than the 101st Airborne Division led by Petraeus."

In February 2004, the 101st was replaced in Mosul by a portion of I Corps headquarters, but operational forces consisted solely of a unit roughly one quarter its size—a ___E:Stryker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stryker)___ brigade.

The largely ___E:Sunni U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sunni)___ ___E:Arab U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab)___ police collapsed under insurgent attacks launched at the same time Coalition Forces attacked ___E:Fallujah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fallujah)___ in November 2004.

On the other hand, in the book Fiasco , The Washington Post reporter Tom Ricks wrote that "Mosul was quiet while he (Petraeus) was there, and likely would have remained so had his successor had as many troops as he had—and as much understanding of counterinsurgency techniques." Army in Iraq was trying to adopt in 2006".

In June 2004, less than six months after the 101st returned to the U.S., Petraeus was promoted to lieutenant general and became the first commander of the ___E:Multi-National Security Transition Command - Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-National_Security_Transition_Command_-_Iraq)___ .

This newly created command had responsibility for training, equipping, and mentoring Iraq's growing army, police, and other security forces, as well as developing Iraq's security institutions and building associated infrastructure, such as training bases, police stations, and border forts.
During Petraeus's fifteen months at the helm of MNSTC-I, he stood up a three-star command virtually from scratch and in the midst of serious fighting in places like Fallujah, Mosul, and Najaf.

By the end of his command, some 100,000 Iraqi Security Forces had been trained; Iraqi Army and Police were being employed in combat; countless reconstruction projects had been executed; and hundreds of thousands of weapons, body armor, and other equipment had been distributed in what was described as the "largest military procurement and distribution effort since World War II", at a cost of over $11 billion.

In September 2004, Petraeus wrote an article for The Washington Post in which he described the tangible progress being made in building Iraq's security forces from the ground up while also noting the many challenges associated with doing so. "Although there have been reverses – not to mention horrific terrorist attacks," Petraeus wrote, "there has been progress in the effort to enable Iraqis to shoulder more of the load for their own security, something they are keen to do."

Some of the challenges involved in building security forces had to do with accomplishing this task in the midst of a tough insurgency—or, as Petraeus wrote, "making the mission akin to repairing an aircraft while in flight—and while being shot at".
Other challenges included allegations of corruption as well as efforts to improve Iraq's supply accountability procedures.

For example, according to former ___E:Interim Iraq Governing Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interim_Iraq_Governing_Council)___ member ___E:Ali A. Allawi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ali_A._Allawi)___ in The Occupation of Iraq: Winning the War, Losing the Peace , "under the very noses of the security transition command, officials both inside and outside the ministry of defense were planning to embezzle most, if not all, of the procurement budget of the army."  The Washington Post stated in August 2007 that ___E:the Pentagon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Pentagon)___ had lost track of approximately 30% of weapons supplied to the Iraqi security forces.

The ___E:General Accounting Office U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Accounting_Office)___ said that the weapons distribution was haphazard, rushed, and did not follow established procedures—particularly from 2004 to 2005, when security training was led by Petraeus and Iraq's security forces began to see combat in places like Najaf and Samarra.

Over a hundred thousand ___E:AK-47 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47)___ ___E:assault rifles U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault_rifle)___ and ___E:pistols U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pistol)___ were delivered to Iraqi forces without full documentation, and some of the missing weapons may have been abducted by ___E:Iraqi insurgents U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraqi_insurgency_(Iraq_War))___ .

Thousands of ___E:body armour U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Body_armour)___ pieces have also been lost.  The Independent stated that the military believed "the situation on the ground was so urgent, and the agency responsible for recording the transfers of arms so short-staffed, that field commanders had little choice in the matter."  The Pentagon conducted its own investigation, and accountability was subsequently regained for many of the weapons.

Following his second tour in Iraq, Petraeus authored a widely read article in Military Review , listing fourteen observations he had made during two tours in Iraq, including: do not do too much with your own hands, money is ammunition, increasing the number of stakeholders is critical to success, success in a counterinsurgency requires more than just military operations, ultimate success depends on local leaders, there is no substitute for flexible and adaptable leaders, and, finally, a leader's most important task is to set the right tone.

The intervening time between the Iraq commands was spent at Fort Leavenworth, where Petraeus further developed his military doctrine and pursued an important White House contact in ___E:Meghan O'Sullivan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meghan_O%27Sullivan)___ who was the principal adviser to the president on the war.  In January 2007, as part of his overhauled Iraq strategy, President ___E:George W. Bush U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush)___ announced that Petraeus would succeed Gen. ___E:George Casey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_William_Casey_Jr.)___ as commanding general of MNF-I to lead all U.S. troops in Iraq. In his memoirs, President Bush likened his selection of Petraeus to the elevations of other great generals of American history, writing, "Lincoln discovered Generals Grant and Sherman.
Roosevelt had Eisenhower and Bradley.
I found David Petraeus and Ray Odierno."

On 23 January, the ___E:Senate Armed Services Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_Armed_Services_Committee)___ held Petraeus's nomination hearing, during which he testified on his ideas for Iraq, particularly the strategy underpinning the " ___E:surge U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War_troop_surge_of_2007)___ " of forces.

During his opening statement, Petraeus stated that "security of the population, especially in Baghdad, and in partnership with the Iraqi Security Forces, will be the focus of the military effort." He went on to state that security would require establishing a persistent presence, especially in Iraq's most threatened neighborhoods.
He also noted the critical importance of helping Iraq increase its governmental capacity, develop employment programs, and improve daily life for its citizens.

Throughout Petraeus's tenure in Iraq, ___E:Multi-National Force-Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-National_Force-Iraq)___ endeavored to work with the ___E:Government of Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq)___ to carry out this strategy that focused on securing the population.

Doing so required establishing—and maintaining—persistent presence by living among the population, separating reconcilable Iraqis from irreconcilable enemies, relentlessly pursuing the enemy, taking back sanctuaries and then holding areas that had been cleared, and continuing to develop Iraq's security forces and to support local security forces, often called ___E:Sons of Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sons_of_Iraq)___ , and integrate them into the Iraqi Army and Police and other employment programs.
The strategy underpinning the "surge" of forces, as well as the ideas Petraeus included in U.S.

Army Field Manual 3–24, Counterinsurgency , have been referred to by some journalists and politicians as the "Petraeus Doctrine", although the surge itself was proposed a few months before Petraeus took command.

Despite the misgivings of most Democratic and a few Republican senators over the proposed implementation of the "Petraeus Doctrine" in Iraq, specifically regarding the troop surge, Petraeus was unanimously confirmed as a four-star general and MNF-I commander on 27 January.

Before leaving for Iraq, Petraeus recruited a number of highly educated military officers, nicknamed "Petraeus guys" or "designated thinkers", to advise him as commander, including Col. Mike Meese, head of the Social Sciences Department at West Point and Col. ___E:H.R. McMaster U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H.R._McMaster)___ , famous for his leadership at the ___E:Battle of 73 Easting U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_73_Easting)___ in the Gulf War and in the pacification of ___E:Tal Afar U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tal_Afar)___ more recently, as well as for his doctoral dissertation on Vietnam-era civil-military relations titled ___E:Dereliction of Duty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dereliction_of_Duty_(1998_book))___ .

While most of Petraeus's closest advisers were American military officers, he also hired Lt. Col. ___E:David Kilcullen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Kilcullen)___ of the ___E:Australian Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Army)___ , who was working for the ___E:U.S. State Department U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._State_Department)___ .
Kilcullen upon his return from Iraq published The Accidental Guerrilla ,  and has discussed the central front of the war and lessons learned in Iraq in The Washington Post .

After taking command of MNF-I on 10 February 2007, Petraeus inspected U.S. and Iraqi units all over Iraq, visiting outposts in greater ___E:Baghdad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baghdad)___ , ___E:Tikrit U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tikrit)___ , ___E:Baquba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baqubah)___ , ___E:Ramadi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramadi)___ , ___E:Mosul U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosul)___ , ___E:Kirkuk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kirkuk)___ , ___E:Bayji U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bayji)___ , ___E:Samarra U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samarra)___ , ___E:Basrah U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basrah)___ and as far west as al-Hit and Al Qaim. In April 2007, Petraeus made his first visit to Washington as MNF-I Commander, reporting to President Bush and Congress on the progress of the "surge" and the overall situation in Iraq. During this visit he met privately with members of Congress and reportedly argued against setting a timetable for U.S. troop withdrawal from Iraq.
By late May 2007, Congress had not imposed any timetables in war funding legislation for troop withdrawal.
The enacted legislation did mandate that Petraeus and the U.S.

Ambassador to Iraq, ___E:Ryan Crocker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Crocker)___ , deliver a report to Congress by 15 September 2007, detailing their assessment of the military, economic and political situation of Iraq.

In June 2007, Petraeus stated in an interview that there were "astonishing signs of normalcy" in Baghdad, and this comment drew criticism from Senate majority leader ___E:Harry Reid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Reid)___ .

In the same interview, however, Petraeus stated that "many problems remain" and he noted the need to help the Iraqis "stitch back together the fabric of society that was torn during the height of sectarian violence" in late 2006.  Petraeus also warned that he expected that the situation in Iraq would require the continued deployment of the elevated troop level of more than 150,000 beyond September 2007; he also stated that U.S. involvement in Iraq could last years afterward.

These statements are representative of the fact that throughout their time in Iraq, Petraeus and Crocker remained circumspect and refused to classify themselves as optimists or pessimists, noting, instead, that they were realists and that the reality in Iraq was very hard. They also repeatedly emphasized the importance of forthright reports and an unvarnished approach.

Indeed, Petraeus's realistic approach and assessments were lauded during the McLaughlin Group's 2008 Year-End Awards, when ___E:Monica Crowley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monica_Crowley)___ nominated Petraeus for the most honest person of the year, stating, "[H]e spoke about the great successes of the surge in Iraq, but he always tempered it, never sugar-coated it."

In July 2007, the ___E:White House U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House)___ submitted to Congress the ___E:interim report on Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Initial_Benchmark_Assessment_Report)___ , which stated that coalition forces had made satisfactory progress on 6 of 18 benchmarks set by Congress.

On 7 September 2007, in a letter addressed to the troops he was commanding, Petraeus wrote that much military progress had been made, but that the national-level political progress that was hoped for had not been achieved.
Petraeus's ___E:Report to Congress on the Situation in Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Report_to_Congress_on_the_Situation_in_Iraq)___ was delivered to Congress on 10 September 2007.

On 15 August 2007, the Los Angeles Times had stated that, according to ___E:unnamed administration officials U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Journalism_sourcing)___ , the report "would actually be written by the ___E:White House U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_W._Bush_Administration)___ , with inputs from officials throughout the government."  However, Petraeus declared in his testimony to Congress that "I wrote this testimony myself." He further elaborated that his testimony to Congress "has not been cleared by, nor shared with, anyone in the Pentagon, the White House, or Congress."

In his September Congressional testimony, Petraeus stated, "As a bottom line up front, the military objectives of the surge are, in large measure, being met." He cited numerous factors for this progress, to include the fact that Coalition and Iraqi Forces had dealt significant blows to Al-Qaeda Iraq and had disrupted Shia militias, that ethno-sectarian violence had been reduced, and that the tribal rejection of Al-Qaeda had spread from Anbar Province to numerous other locations across Iraq. Based on this progress and additional progress expected to be achieved, Petraeus recommended drawing down the surge forces from Iraq and gradually transitioning increased responsibilities to Iraqi Forces, as their capabilities and conditions on the ground permitted.

___E:Democratic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Democratic_Party)___ ___E:Senate Majority Leader U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_leaders_of_the_United_States_Senate)___ ___E:Harry Reid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_Reid)___ of ___E:Nevada U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nevada)___ argued Petraeus's "plan is just more of the same" and "is neither a drawdown or a change in mission that we need." Chairman of the ___E:House Foreign Affairs Committee U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_Foreign_Affairs_Committee)___ ___E:Tom Lantos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tom_Lantos)___ of ___E:California U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California)___ called Petraeus and ___E:U.S. Ambassador to Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_Iraq)___ ___E:Ryan Crocker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Crocker)___ "two of our nation's most capable ___E:public servants U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_servants)___ " and said Democrats feel "esteem for their ___E:professionalism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Professionalism)___ ".

___E:Republican U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Republican_Party)___ ___E:Presidential candidate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Republican_presidential_candidates,_2008)___ ___E:Duncan Hunter U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_L._Hunter)___ called the report "a candid, independent assessment given with integrity".

A USA Today / ___E:Gallup poll U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallup_poll)___ taken after Petraeus's report to Congress showed virtually no change in negative public opinion toward the war. On 20 September, the Senate passed an amendment by Republican ___E:John Cornyn III U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Cornyn_III)___ of ___E:Texas U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texas)___ designed to "strongly condemn personal attacks on the honor and integrity of General Petraeus".

It now looks as if Petraeus was broadly right on this issue at least."

Based on the conditions on the ground, in October 2007, Petraeus and ___E:U.S. Ambassador to Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Ambassador_to_Iraq)___ ___E:Ryan Crocker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ryan_Crocker)___ revised their campaign plan for Iraq. On 18 February 2008, USA Today stated that "the U.S. effort has shown more success" and that, after the number of troops reached its peak in fall 2007, "U.S. deaths were at their lowest levels since the 2003 invasion, civilian casualties were down, and street life was resuming in Baghdad."  In light of the significant reduction in violence and as the surge brigades began to redeploy without replacement, Petraeus characterized the progress as tenuous, fragile, and reversible and repeatedly reminded all involved that much work remained to be done.   During an early February trip to Iraq, Defense Secretary ___E:Robert Gates U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Gates)___ endorsed the idea of a period of consolidation and evaluation upon completion of the withdrawal of surge brigades from Iraq.
Petraeus and Crocker continued these themes at their two full days of testimony before Congress on 8–9 April.

During his opening statement, Petraeus stated that "there has been significant but uneven security progress in Iraq", while also noting that "the situation in certain areas is still unsatisfactory and that innumerable challenges remain" and that "the progress made since last spring is fragile and reversible." He also recommended a continuation of the drawdown of surge forces as well as a 45-day period of consolidation and evaluation after the final surge brigade had redeployed in late July.  Analysts for USA Today and The New York Times stated that the hearings "lacked the suspense of last September's debate," but they did include sharp questioning as well as both skepticism and praise from various Congressional leaders.

Petraeus also noted that during the week before his testimony, the number of security incidents in Iraq was the lowest in over four years.

After Petraeus's return to Baghdad, and despite the continued drawdown of surge forces as well as recent Iraqi-led operations in places like Basrah, Mosul, and Baghdad, the number of security incidents in Iraq remained at their lowest level in over four years.

In September 2008, Petraeus gave an interview to ___E:BBC News U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_News)___ stating that he did not think using the term "victory" in describing the Iraq war was appropriate, saying "This is not the sort of struggle where you take a hill, plant the flag and go home to a victory parade ... it's not war with a simple slogan."

On the eve of his change of command, in September 2008, Petraeus stated that "I don't use terms like victory or defeat ...
I'm a realist, not an optimist or a pessimist.
And the reality is that there has been significant progress but there are still serious challenges."

Gates also told Petraeus he believed "history will regard you as one of our nation's greatest battle captains."  He presented Petraeus with the ___E:Defense Distinguished Service Medal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_Distinguished_Service_Medal)___ .

At the event, Petraeus mentioned the difficulty in getting the ___E:Sons of Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sons_of_Iraq)___ absorbed into the central ___E:Government of Iraq U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Iraq)___ and warned about future consequences if the effort stalled.

When speaking of these and other challenges, Petraeus noted that "the gains [achieved in Iraq] are tenuous and unlikely to survive without an American effort that outlasts his tenure." Even so, as Petraeus departed Iraq, it appeared to many that he was leaving a much different Iraq than the one that existed when he took command in February 2007. As described by Dexter Filkins, "violence has plummeted from its apocalyptic peaks, Iraqi leaders are asserting themselves, and streets that once seemed dead are flourishing with life."  The 3 January 2009, Iraq Trends (a chart produced weekly by the MNF-I) seemed to illustrate an increase in incidents followed by the sharp decline described by Dexter Filkens and others.
Petraeus' command of coalition forces during the Surge in Iraq was lauded by a number of observers.

In his book The Savior Generals historian ___E:Victor Davis Hanson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Davis_Hanson)___ wrote, "that without David Petraeus, the American effort in Iraq—along with the reputation of the U.S. military in the Middle East—would have been lost long ago." In an interview for Newsweek magazine's "Interview Issue: The View From People Who Make a Difference," Petraeus expressed his support for President Obama's announced Afghanistan strategy and discussed his view that reconciliation efforts in Afghanistan should for the time being occur "at the lower and midlevels".

He expressed doubt that the U.S. would become involved in the country while the Taliban was in power, outside of military and intelligence actions to protect U.S. interests, and suggested that even the establishment of an embassy for diplomatic relations would not happen "any time soon".

Petraeus has been vocally critical of ___E:Russia's invasion of Ukraine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine)___ , joining three other retired military generals to form the Strategic Advisory Council for the Defense of Ukraine in July 2022 to provide strategic expertise and operational assistance to Ukrainian forces.

On 12 March 2022, Petraeus spoke on One Nation with Brian Kilmeade, criticizing the Russian military's failed attempt to achieve a ___E:combined arms U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combined_arms)___ effect, which, according to Petraeus, wasn't up to the normal standards anticipated by the United States or other NATO countries' militaries.
In May 2022, Petraeus commented that, in an attempt to create a stronger Russia, President Putin had instead strengthened the alliance between NATO countries.

In a later interview, Petraeus said that the Russian military was nowhere near as good as NATO had thought it would be.  He described the Russian military's preferred tactic as that of overwhelming artillery strikes, leading to the question of whether Russia's military valued volume over accuracy.
In October 2022, he called Russia's military mobilization in Ukraine "irreversible and disastrous".

In addition to criticisms of Russia's war effort, Petraeus also discussed the negative implications that Russian sanctions have for worldwide financial markets, food supplies, and other commodities, and he commended the Ukrainian military for its impressive counter-attacks, specifically a raid on Russian tanks, the killing of five Russian generals, and the destruction of the Russian warship, Saratov.
In mid- to late 2022, Petraeus spoke further on the Western response to Russia's aggression and the impacts U.S. involvement had on Ukraine's defense.

In an interview with CNN's ___E:Jim Sciutto U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Sciutto)___ regarding Russia's plans to annex more regions in Ukraine, he said that US- and UK-supplied high-mobility artillery rocket systems had prompted Russian forces to relocate their headquarters and fuel supplies, which had significantly slowed Russia's advances in Ukraine.
In another interview, he said that Western support had improved counteroffensive strategies, resulting in retaking Crimea and Donbas territories from Russia.
Petraeus has been a strong proponent of continued aid to Ukraine and increased NATO readiness for potential escalations by Russia and its allies.

He spoke of the need for the United States to prioritize military readiness to counter China and to increase aid for Ukraine in the annual defense policy bill.  He also discussed the importance of deploying Patriot missile systems in Ukraine as an anti-ballistic missile system and discussed measures that the US and NATO would employ if Russia were to carry out a nuclear attack in Ukraine.

In an Atlantic Council discussion concerning additional aid to Ukraine he emphasized the need for the deployment of Western aircraft and support staff, a stronger defense guarantee, and diplomatic and economic pressures on Russia to hasten peace talks.
Petraeus expressed the belief that President Putin would eventually realize that the war is not sustainable on the battlefield and would agree to a negotiated resolution with Ukraine.
In an article published by Foreign Policy magazine, Petraeus joined other experts to derive lessons from the Russian-Ukraine war that would prevent, deter, and combat forthcoming world conflicts.

During a trip to Kyiv, Petraeus joined a group from the Atlantic Council in presenting the council's Global Citizen Award to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, recognizing his exceptional leadership in defending Ukraine against Russian aggression.

He emphasized the effectiveness of Ukraine's newly formed brigades equipped with Western tanks and fighting vehicles, offering valuable insights and support to Ukraine's efforts in countering the Russian forces.

In an interview with CNN, Petraeus shared his view that alleged Ukrainian ___E:drone attacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drone_warfare)___ on Russian soil were a way to not only attack valid military targets but also to acquaint the Russian people with the fact that a war was happening.
He also described a shift in the Ukrainian strategy in their summer offensive as "starve, stretch and strike," a tactic used to create greater opportunity for success later in the conflict.

Speaking with CNN's Christiane Amanpour in response to the slow pace of Ukraine's counteroffensive in the summer of 2023, Petraeus noted that while the Russian military hadn't distinguished itself in many ways, the depth of their defenses in territory seized in Ukraine had proven formidable.
In the same interview, he stated his opinion that Ukraine's forces had adapted well to Russian entrenchment, taking their time to pick through mine fields without the aid of air support.
Petraeus once again argued for more military aid for Ukraine, and increased sanctions against Russia, in an effort to force a diplomatic resolution to the conflict.

In another conversation with Amanpour, he warned that if Putin succeeds in achieving his substantial objectives in Ukraine, then Moldova or one of the Baltic states could be invaded next.
